parts.partTitle: Why Sealed Classes Beat Open Inheritance

beats.headline: Why is your switch statement failing silently?
beats.subline: Open hierarchies let anyone add subtypes, breaking your logic without a compiler error.
beats.narration: Open class hierarchies are a liability. When you use a standard abstract class, any developer can add a new subtype in a distant package. Your existing switch statements won't know, and your logic will silently fail in production.

beats.title: Open vs. Closed Hierarchies

top.label: Open (Standard)

bottom.label: Sealed (Java 17+)
bottom.code:
public sealed interface Status
    permits Success, Failed {}

beats.narration: Sealed classes turn your domain model into a finite set. By using the permits clause, you tell the compiler exactly which classes are allowed. If a new type is added, the compiler forces you to handle it everywhere.

beats.title: Defining a Sealed Hierarchy

steps.explanation: Restricts the hierarchy to a specific list of permitted subtypes.
The explicit list of allowed implementations. Must reside in the same package.
Records are implicitly final, making them the perfect fit for sealed sum types.

beats.narration: The sealed keyword restricts the hierarchy. The permits clause defines the exact list of allowed subtypes. Since records are implicitly final, they pair perfectly with sealed interfaces to create rock-solid domain models.

beats.title: Sum Types + Product Types
beats.subtitle: Algebraic Data Types in Java

nodes.label: Sealed Interface
nodes.detail: Sum Type: Fixed set of alternatives

nodes.label: Compiler
nodes.detail: Verifies exhaustiveness across the whole set

beats.narration: You are building Algebraic Data Types. Sealed interfaces act as Sum Types, representing a fixed set of possibilities, while records act as Product Types, bundling data. The compiler ties them together for total safety.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.narration: Sealed classes are the foundation. In Part 2, we see how Java 21's exhaustive switch pattern matching eliminates the need for default branches and runtime errors.

beats.headline: Stop using default branches in your switch.
beats.subline: If you use a sealed type, the compiler already knows every possible case.
beats.narration: Stop using default branches in your switch statements. If you are switching over a sealed type, the compiler already knows every possible case. A default branch just hides bugs when you add new types later.

beats.title: Exhaustive Switch Expression

steps.explanation: Returns a value directly, forcing you to handle all cases.
Unpacks the type and binds the variable in one step.
If you add a new subtype to the sealed interface, this code will fail to compile.

beats.narration: This switch expression is exhaustive. If you add a new permitted subtype to your interface, the compiler will instantly flag every switch statement that needs an update. No more missed branches in production.

beats.title: Record Deconstruction

steps.explanation: Extracts fields directly from the record without calling getters.
Adds conditional logic to your pattern match.

beats.narration: Record patterns let you deconstruct objects directly in the case label. Combine this with when guards to filter by value. It is clean, readable, and keeps your logic close to the data structure.

beats.title: Pattern Matching vs. Old Way

top.label: Old instanceof

bottom.label: Pattern Match
bottom.code:
case Success(var ts, var ref) -> 
    process(ref);

beats.narration: Compare this to the old instanceof chains. You no longer need to manually cast objects or check types. Pattern matching handles the extraction and the type check in a single, readable line.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): JVM Internals & Reflection Safety →
beats.narration: Exhaustive switches are a game changer. In Part 3, we look at how the JVM enforces these rules at runtime and why reflection can't bypass your sealed hierarchy.

beats.headline: Can you bypass sealed classes with reflection?
beats.subline: The JVM enforces your hierarchy at the class-loading level.
beats.narration: Think you can bypass sealed classes with reflection or custom bytecode? Think again. The JVM enforces your hierarchy at the class-loading level. If a class isn't in the permitted list, the JVM refuses to load it.

beats.title: Inspecting PermittedSubclasses
beats.caption: The binary contract in the classfile

lines.text: # JVM checks this list at runtime!

beats.narration: When you compile a sealed class, the compiler adds a PermittedSubclasses attribute to the bytecode. The JVM reads this attribute during class loading. If an unauthorized class tries to extend your sealed type, the JVM throws an IncompatibleClassChangeError.

beats.title: Runtime Enforcement
beats.subtitle: The JVM Class Loader Security

nodes.label: Class Loader
nodes.detail: Loads the class and inspects supertype

nodes.label: PermittedSubclasses
nodes.detail: JVM verifies the class is in the list

beats.narration: The JVM is the final authority. It checks the PermittedSubclasses attribute before allowing any class to link against your sealed type. This isn't just a compile-time suggestion; it is a hard runtime guarantee.

beats.title: The non-sealed Escape Hatch

steps.explanation: Allows any class to extend this specific branch while keeping the parent sealed.

beats.narration: Need an escape hatch? Use non-sealed. It allows you to re-open a specific branch of your hierarchy for plugins or external extensions, while the top-level interface remains sealed and exhaustive.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Replacing the Visitor Pattern →
beats.narration: The JVM has your back. In Part 4, we finish by replacing the bulky Visitor pattern with clean, modern sealed hierarchies and pattern matching.

beats.headline: Delete your Visitor pattern boilerplate.
beats.subline: Sealed classes and pattern matching do the same job with 80% less code.
beats.narration: Delete your Visitor pattern boilerplate. It was a necessary evil to handle closed hierarchies in old Java. Now, sealed classes and pattern matching do the same job with 80% less code and better readability.

beats.title: Visitor vs. Pattern Matching

top.label: Visitor Pattern
top.code:
interface Visitor { visit(Add a); }
class Add { accept(Visitor v) { v.visit(this); } }

bottom.label: Pattern Match

beats.narration: The Visitor pattern requires double dispatch and massive interfaces. Pattern matching treats your data as pure data, allowing you to write operations as simple methods. It is cleaner, faster, and much easier to debug.

beats.title: One-Line Simplification

steps.explanation: Matches deep object graphs in a single expression.
Returns a new object based on the matched structure.

beats.narration: Look at this nested match. You can fold constant additions in one line. This is impossible with the Visitor pattern without creating complex, stateful traversal logic. Pattern matching makes tree transformations trivial.

beats.title: The Expression Problem
beats.subtitle: Choosing your design strategy

nodes.label: Open Interface
nodes.detail: Easy to add new types, hard to add new operations

nodes.label: Sealed Hierarchy
nodes.detail: Easy to add new operations, hard to add new types

nodes.label: Trade-off
nodes.detail: Pick the strategy that fits your growth

beats.narration: Choose your strategy based on the Expression Problem. Use open interfaces for plugin architectures. Use sealed hierarchies when your domain model is stable and you need to add many operations like serialization or evaluation.
